COLDWAR_SOV_nt_molodaya_gvardiya: Published by the Komsomol's own press, the journal Molodaya Gvardiya has become the mouthpiece of the so-called Russian Party: writers and editors who praise village life, Orthodox heritage and the greatness of the Russian nation. Opening its pages wider would give Russian nationalists a respectable platform inside the Soviet system, at the price of unsettling the other republics.
COLDWAR_SOV_nt_the_victory_cult: Since 1965, Victory Day is once again a public holiday, and the memory of the Great Patriotic War has become the strongest shared faith of the Soviet people. From the Motherland Calls on Mamayev Kurgan to the eternal flames in every town, twenty million dead bind the nation together. Raising the victory above the revolution itself would make the sacrifice of the Russian people the true foundation of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_nt_vozrozhdenie: Beneath the official slogans, a quiet current runs through Soviet Russia: restored churches and monasteries, the village prose of Valentin Rasputin and Vasily Belov, the All-Russian Society for the Protection of Historical and Cultural Monuments. Its followers speak of a vozrozhdenie, a rebirth of the Russian nation after decades of uprooting. Embracing this revival would turn cultural nostalgia into a political programme.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_russian_party: For years the Russian Party worked in the shadows of the Central Committee, in editorial offices and Komsomol cells. Now its patrons step forward openly, promising that Russia will no longer pay for the other nations of the union and will finally be master in its own house. The transfer of power will shake the apparatus, and the republics will watch with deep unease.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_national_rebirth: In the darkest corner of the Russian Party, radicals dream of more than a reformed union: a Committee of National Rebirth that would sweep away the Marxist creed entirely and rebuild Russia as an ethnic, authoritarian state. What if a deep crisis of the system handed them their moment? Such a seizure of power would break with everything Soviet and could tear the union apart.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_marshals: The Soviet marshals have always stood just outside the circle of power, mindful of how Zhukov was cast aside in 1957. Should the Party falter and the country slide into disorder, the High Command could step in as guardian of the state, ruling through a council of marshals in the name of order and the great victory. The army's loyalty would then belong to the nation rather than to the Party.
COLDWAR_SOV_power_romanovs: Half a century after Yekaterinburg, the idea seems absurd: a Romanov back in the Kremlin. Yet in emigre circles in France and Spain, Grand Duke Vladimir Kirillovich still claims the throne, and among disillusioned Russian nationalists the old symbols are quietly regaining their pull. What if a collapsing order turned to the crown as the last remaining source of legitimacy?
COLDWAR_SOV_nt_russia_first: Why should Russian workers pay for cotton in Uzbekistan and new factories in the Baltic while the villages of the Non-Black Earth region decay? The question is asked ever more openly in Moscow. Putting Russia first means redirecting investment, prestige and political attention to the Russian heartland, even if the other republics see it as a betrayal of the union's promise.
COLDWAR_SOV_nt_the_rsfsr_institutions: Every Soviet republic has its own Communist Party, its own Academy of Sciences and its own KGB, every one except Russia, whose affairs are run directly by the all-union centre. Russian nationalists have long called this a humiliation. Creating separate Russian institutions would give the largest republic a voice of its own, but also a power base that could one day rival the union itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_nt_the_army_of_the_nation: Officially, the Soviet Army belongs to all Soviet peoples, but its officer corps is overwhelmingly Russian and its traditions reach back to Suvorov and Kutuzov. Nationalists want to make that heritage explicit: an army rooted in Russian history, Russian valour and Russian soil rather than in proletarian internationalism. Soldiers who fight for the motherland, they argue, fight harder than those who fight for an abstraction.
COLDWAR_SOV_nt_the_imperial_question: Every Russian nationalist must eventually answer the same question: is the Soviet Union Russia's empire, to be held at any cost, or a burden that drains the Russian nation? One camp would keep every republic by force if needed; the other would let the restless periphery go and build a tighter union around the Slavic core. The answer will define the country's borders for generations.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_the_party_of_lenin: Nearly fifteen million members strong, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union is the spine of the state, the guardian of Lenin's legacy and the source of every career that matters. As the country enters the 1970s, the leadership must decide how the Party presents itself: as a living revolutionary vanguard or as the steady administrator of a mature socialist society. Either way, its authority must remain beyond question.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_the_nomenklatura: The nomenklatura lists decide who runs every factory, ministry, newspaper and regional committee in the Soviet Union. Those on them enjoy special shops, dachas and the certainty that their position is safe. Strengthening this system binds the cadres firmly to the Party, but it also breeds a privileged caste that grows ever more comfortable and ever less accountable.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_the_komsomol: With nearly thirty million members, the Leninist Young Communist League is the Party's school and recruiting ground. Its brigades raise new towns in Siberia, its activists organise every university and factory, and its leaders are the next generation of the nomenklatura. A revitalised Komsomol could bind Soviet youth to the cause, if it can still inspire rather than merely organise.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_the_party_card_exchange: The 24th Party Congress has decided that every Communist must receive a new party card, and in 1973 and 1974 each member has to appear in person to exchange the old one. Officially it is an administrative procedure; in practice it is a quiet purge, as the passive, the corrupt and the drunk can simply be left without a new card. Done seriously, the exchange could cleanse the ranks without the terror of earlier decades.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_democratic_centralism: Lenin's principle of democratic centralism holds that debate is free until a decision is made, and that afterwards every member must carry it out without dissent. In practice, the emphasis has long fallen on centralism. Reaffirming the doctrine closes the ranks behind the Politburo's line and shields the Party against factions and foreign ideas, though it leaves little room for initiative from below.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_the_constitution_of_dev: A new Soviet constitution, long prepared by a commission under Brezhnev himself, could name the Party outright as 'the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, the nucleus of its political system'. The basic law would enshrine the era of developed socialism and the Party's monopoly in a single article. Written into law, the Party's role would no longer be a matter of practice but of constitutional principle.
COLDWAR_SOV_cpsu_the_party_of_the_whole_: Since Khrushchev's programme of 1961, the CPSU no longer calls itself merely the party of the working class but the party of the whole Soviet people. With the dictatorship of the proletariat declared complete, it claims to speak for workers, collective farmers and the intelligentsia alike, and for every nation of the union. Embracing this broad identity widens its base, at the cost of some revolutionary sharpness.
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_the_politburo: Real power in the Soviet Union lies with a dozen elderly men around a table in the Kremlin Senate. Since Khrushchev's fall in 1964, Leonid Brezhnev has ruled as first among equals, balancing Kosygin's government, Suslov's ideology and the ambitions of younger rivals. Every succession, every change of course and every career is decided here, behind closed doors and by a show of hands.
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_kos: Alexei Kosygin has headed the Council of Ministers since 1964 and is respected at home and abroad as a capable manager. His economic reform of 1965, however, is being slowly strangled by the Party apparatus. What if the Premier's allies in the ministries and the Central Committee called a plenum to make him General Secretary, placing the government's pragmatism above the Party's ideology?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_pod: As Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, Nikolai Podgorny is the formal head of the Soviet state and the third man of the collective leadership. A veteran of the Kharkov party organisation and former leader of the Ukrainian Communists, he commands loyalties in the largest non-Russian republic. What if a plenum turned to him, raising the organs of the state above the Party secretariat?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_sus: Mikhail Suslov, the Party's chief ideologist, has never sought the top post, preferring to guard doctrine from the shadows, which has earned him the name 'grey cardinal'. Ascetic, dogmatic and feared, he has made and broken careers for more than two decades. What if a plenum asked him to step forward and personally steer the Party back towards ideological purity?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_she: Alexander Shelepin, once head of the Komsomol and later of the KGB, helped topple Khrushchev in 1964 and was soon seen as Brezhnev's most dangerous rival. Since 1967 he has been sidelined to the trade unions, yet 'Iron Shurik' still has friends among the security men and the former Komsomol generation. What if a plenum brought him back to finish what he began, with an iron broom for the cadres?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_and: Yuri Andropov has run the KGB since 1967 and knows more about the Party's secrets, and its corruption, than anyone else in the leadership. Austere, intelligent and patient, he is the candidate of those who believe the country needs discipline and order before anything else. Historically he succeeded Brezhnev in November 1982, but a plenum could bring the Chekist to power much sooner.
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_gre: Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence since 1967, speaks for an army that has made the Soviet Union a military superpower. Blunt and hawkish, he distrusts detente and the civilians who negotiate it. What if the Politburo, fearing weakness abroad and drift at home, handed the Party to a soldier for the first time, with the General Staff standing firmly behind him?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_ust: Dmitry Ustinov became People's Commissar for Armaments in 1941, at just thirty-two, and has overseen the Soviet defence industry ever since, from tanks and artillery to missiles and space rockets. As Central Committee Secretary for defence, he is the patron of the military-industrial complex. What if a plenum chose the armourer himself, placing the needs of the defence plants at the centre of the state?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_gro: Grigory Romanov, the rising master of the Leningrad party organisation, rules the second city of the Soviet Union with a firm hand and a close eye on the defence factories that fill it. Young by Politburo standards, orthodox and efficient, he is already spoken of as a future leader. What if a plenum skipped a generation and summoned the man from Smolny to the Kremlin?
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_che: Konstantin Chernenko has spent his career at Brezhnev's side, rising from propaganda work in Moldavia to head the Central Committee's General Department. He has no power base of his own beyond the apparatus, which is precisely why the old guard trusts him. Historically he succeeded Andropov in February 1984; a plenum could make the loyal apparatchik leader whenever the elders want continuity above all.
COLDWAR_SOV_ple_gor: Mikhail Gorbachev, the energetic party chief of Stavropol, belongs to a generation shaped by Khrushchev's thaw rather than by Stalin's purges. Powerful patrons such as Andropov and Suslov have marked him as a man of the future. Historically he became General Secretary in March 1985; a plenum could hand power to the new generation earlier, with all the hope and risk that change brings.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_dear_leonid_ilyich: Since October 1964, Leonid Ilyich Brezhnev has led the Party, first cautiously, then with growing confidence. After the upheavals of Stalin and Khrushchev, he offers the nomenklatura what it craves most: stability, predictability and respect for its positions. Hailed as 'dear Leonid Ilyich' in official speeches, he now stands ready to shape a whole era in his own image.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_dnepropetrovsk_clan: Brezhnev built his career in Dnepropetrovsk and Moldavia, and the men he met there have followed him to Moscow: Andrei Kirilenko in the Secretariat, Nikolai Shchelokov at the Interior Ministry, Nikolai Tikhonov in the Council of Ministers. Promoting this circle of old comrades secures the General Secretary's grip on key posts, but it also rewards loyalty above competence.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_general_department: Every document that reaches the Politburo passes through the Central Committee's General Department, headed since 1965 by Konstantin Chernenko. He controls the agenda, the minutes and the flow of paper to the General Secretary's desk. Turning this office into the nerve centre of the leadership makes the bureaucracy run more smoothly and makes Brezhnev's most loyal aide indispensable.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_balance_the_troika: The collective leadership born in 1964 rests on a careful division: Brezhnev leads the Party, Kosygin the government and Podgorny the state. Each has his own clients and ambitions, and open rivalry would threaten everything. By balancing the troika, giving each man a sphere and none a reason to rebel, Brezhnev keeps the peace in the Politburo while quietly strengthening his own position.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_first_choice: The invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 has shown the world that Moscow will defend socialism in Eastern Europe by force. Now the leadership must decide how to use the strategic parity it has reached with the United States. Should it negotiate from strength and harvest the fruits of detente, or harden the Brezhnev Doctrine and confront the West wherever it challenges the socialist camp?
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_detente_from_strength: With nuclear parity achieved, Brezhnev believes the Soviet Union can finally negotiate with the West as an equal. Arms control, trade agreements and summits are not a sign of weakness but proof that the correlation of forces has shifted in favour of socialism. Detente from strength promises Western technology and grain while the Soviet Union keeps its military might intact.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_crimean_talks: In September 1971, Brezhnev invites West German Chancellor Willy Brandt to his dacha at Oreanda in the Crimea. Between swims in the Black Sea and long conversations, the two men confirm the spirit of the Moscow Treaty and of Bonn's new eastern policy. Courting West Germany opens a door to credit and technology and drives a wedge into the Western alliance.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_brezhnev_in_washington: In June 1973, Brezhnev travels to the United States for a second summit with Richard Nixon, a year after their breakthrough meeting in Moscow. On the table lies an Agreement on the Prevention of Nuclear War, committing both superpowers to consult rather than slide into confrontation. Whether Washington signs depends on its own calculations, but the visit itself is a triumph of Soviet prestige.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_helsinki_triumph: In August 1975, thirty-five states sign the Final Act of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in Helsinki. For Brezhnev, it is the crowning achievement of his career: the post-war borders of Europe, including the division of Germany and the Soviet gains of 1945, are recognised as inviolable. The human rights clauses of the third basket seem a small price to pay, for now.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_doctrine_hawk: Prague in 1968 proved that the socialist commonwealth is a single body and that the loss of any part threatens the whole. The hawks around Suslov, Grechko and the General Staff argue that detente is a Western trap and that the Brezhnev Doctrine must guide Soviet policy. Choosing the doctrine means standing firm everywhere and trusting military power over Western goodwill.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_iron_bloc: The Warsaw Pact and Comecon bind Eastern Europe to Moscow, yet Romania goes its own way, Poland simmers and Hungary experiments with markets. An iron bloc would tighten the reins: joint command structures, deeper economic integration and Soviet advisers in every allied defence ministry. The allies would gain security and lose what little room for manoeuvre they still have.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_answer_every_challenge: For every American carrier a Soviet cruiser, for every new missile a Soviet reply. Under this principle, the Soviet Union matches each Western weapons programme step by step, determined never again to suffer the inferiority of the Cuban crisis years. The military-industrial complex welcomes the orders, even as the arms race tightens with every turn.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_internationalist_dut: From Vietnam to Africa and the Middle East, national liberation movements look to Moscow for weapons, advisers and money. Soviet ideologists call it the internationalist duty of the first socialist state to support every people fighting imperialism. Embracing this duty spreads Soviet influence across the Third World, but it also deepens commitments in distant wars with uncertain outcomes.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_tula_speech: In January 1977, presenting Tula with its title of Hero City, Brezhnev declares that the Soviet Union does not seek military superiority and wants only a defence sufficient to deter any attacker. The marshals grumble, but the speech is meant to reassure a new American administration and keep detente alive. Words, however, must be matched by deeds to be believed.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_second_choice: Growth is slowing, and the leadership can no longer fund everything at once. The consumer wants flats, cars and full shelves; the marshals want tanks and missiles; and the new oil fields of Western Siberia promise a flood of hard currency. As the five-year plans of the 1970s take shape, Brezhnev must decide where the Soviet Union places its bet for the coming decade.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_consumer_socialism: The Ninth Five-Year Plan is the first to promise that consumer goods will grow faster than heavy industry. Refrigerators, televisions and the new Zhiguli cars from Togliatti are meant to prove that socialism can deliver a good life, not just steel and rockets. Putting the consumer first buys the contentment of the population, though it strains a planning system built for tanks and turbines.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_little_deal: The economist James Millar would later call it the 'little deal': the regime tolerates the black market, private plots, favours and petty theft, and in return the population tolerates the regime. Accepting this unspoken bargain keeps private life supplied and tempers discontent, while corruption seeps ever deeper into the foundations of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_a_flat_for_every_family: Millions of Soviet families still live in communal apartments, sharing one kitchen between several households. The Party has promised every family a flat of its own, and new prefabricated districts are rising on the edge of every city, from Moscow to Novosibirsk. Pushing housing construction even harder would answer one of the people's deepest wishes and turn a promise into concrete.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_guns_before_butter: The marshals and the defence ministries argue that the international situation leaves no room for indulgence. As long as the United States arms itself and China threatens the Far East, every rouble belongs first to the armed forces. Placing guns before butter guarantees the strength of the military-industrial complex, while the queues for meat and shoes grow longer.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_military_industrial_: The Military-Industrial Commission of the Council of Ministers coordinates the nine defence ministries that build everything from rifles to intercontinental missiles. Giving it greater authority and new factories would turn the defence sector into an even more privileged state within the state. Its output would rise, but so would its claim on the country's best engineers and resources.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_tank_parks: Behind barbed wire across the western military districts and Eastern Europe stand vast tank parks, row upon row of T-55s and T-62s, with the new T-64 entering service. Soviet doctrine counts on overwhelming armoured mass to reach the Rhine within days. Expanding these parks and pushing the next generation of main battle tanks would cement Soviet superiority on land.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_oil_bet: The discovery of Samotlor and the other giant fields of Western Siberia has turned the Soviet Union into an oil power. Exporting crude and gas for hard currency could pay for Western machinery and grain without painful reforms. Betting on oil is the easy road, but an economy that lives off its wells may lose the will to modernise itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_oil_for_grain: Soviet agriculture cannot keep pace with demand, and a single bad harvest, as in 1972, forces Moscow to buy millions of tonnes of grain abroad. Oil money offers a way out: sell crude on the world market and buy wheat, fodder and meat in return. The collective farms gain breathing space and the cities stay fed, as long as oil prices remain high.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_pipelines_to_europe: In 1970, Moscow and Bonn sign the first gas-for-pipes deal: German steel pipes in exchange for Soviet natural gas delivered over twenty years. Austria already receives Soviet gas, and Italy and France are interested in similar contracts. Long-term supply agreements with Western Europe would bring a steady flow of hard currency and bind the continent's industry to Soviet energy, whether NATO likes it or not.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_kgb_or_mvd: Two men compete to be the guardian of Soviet order. Yuri Andropov's KGB watches dissidents, foreign spies and, increasingly, corrupt officials; Nikolai Shchelokov's Interior Ministry runs the militia and enjoys Brezhnev's personal friendship. Their rivalry is bitter and personal. The General Secretary must decide whose methods, and whose people, he will trust to keep the country in line.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_back_the_kgb: Andropov argues that corruption and indiscipline are eating away at the state, and that only the KGB has the reach and the integrity to stop it. Backing the Committee for State Security gives it a free hand to investigate economic crimes, even among the protected clients of regional party bosses. Order will improve, though many in the nomenklatura will learn to fear the knock at the door.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_back_the_mvd: Nikolai Shchelokov has modernised the militia, raised its pay and polished its image with popular television detective series. He is also an old friend of Brezhnev from Moldavia and Dnepropetrovsk. Backing the Interior Ministry means a loyal, comfortable police force that keeps the streets calm, and one that looks the other way when the right people are involved.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_trust_the_republics: Under Brezhnev's stability of cadres, the first secretaries of the union republics enjoy unprecedented security: Sharaf Rashidov in Uzbekistan, Dinmukhamed Kunaev in Kazakhstan, Heydar Aliyev in Azerbaijan. In exchange for loyalty and good plan figures, Moscow asks few questions about how they run their domains. Trusting the republican cadres keeps the union quiet, but lets local patronage networks flourish.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_malaya_zemlya: In 1978, a slim volume of war memoirs appears under Brezhnev's name, celebrating the small bridgehead of Malaya Zemlya near Novorossiysk as if it had decided the war. Printed in millions of copies, it is studied in schools and honoured with the Lenin Prize for Literature. Together with the ever-growing collection of medals on his chest, it marks a personality cult that the nation increasingly mocks in private.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_marshal_brezhnev: In May 1976, Brezhnev is made a Marshal of the Soviet Union, a rank far above the one he held in the war, which he ended as a major general and political officer. The new title flatters the army and ties the General Secretary to its glory. The generals salute, even if some privately resent seeing their highest honour bestowed upon a former political commissar.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_chairman_of_the_presidiu: In June 1977, Nikolai Podgorny is abruptly removed from the Politburo and from his post as head of state, and Brezhnev takes the chairmanship of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet himself. For the first time, one man holds both the leadership of the Party and the formal presidency of the Soviet state. The troika is over; Brezhnev now stands alone at the summit.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_leaders_health: Behind the medals and the ovations, Brezhnev's health is failing. Strokes, a dependence on sleeping pills and increasingly slurred speech turn every public appearance into an ordeal watched closely by foreign diplomats and the Politburo alike. The leadership must decide how to handle the decline: hide it and carry on, or prepare for an orderly departure.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_kremlin_doctors: Yevgeny Chazov and the Fourth Main Directorate of the Ministry of Health, the Kremlin's own medical service, are tasked with keeping the General Secretary on his feet. With the best physicians, private clinics and constant supervision, they can sustain Brezhnev for years, historically until 1982. The leader stays in office, but the country is governed ever more by his aides.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_a_dignified_retirement: More than once, a tired and ailing Brezhnev asks his comrades to let him retire. The Politburo has always refused, fearing a destabilising struggle for the succession. What if this time they agreed? A dignified retirement, with full honours and a chosen successor, would give the Soviet Union something it has never had: a peaceful, planned transfer of power at the very top.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_the_succession: Whoever controls the succession controls the future of the Soviet Union. Andropov has the KGB, Chernenko the apparatus, Romanov the Leningrad organisation, and the young Gorbachev the favour of the reformers. By naming an heir while he still can, Brezhnev may spare the country a struggle in the Politburo, or ignite one.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_heir_andropov: Yuri Andropov is the most capable and the most feared man in the Politburo. Naming him heir promises a successor who will root out corruption and restore discipline, provided the Party is ready for a Chekist at its head. Historically, Andropov succeeded Brezhnev in 1982, after first moving from the KGB back into the Central Committee Secretariat.
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_heir_chernenko: Konstantin Chernenko is Brezhnev's shadow, his most loyal aide and the keeper of his papers. Naming him heir guarantees that nothing will change: the cadres keep their posts, the policies continue and the old guard sleeps soundly. What if Chernenko came to power directly, without Andropov's interlude, and continuity became the Soviet Union's only programme?
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_heir_romanov: Grigory Romanov, the strict and efficient master of Leningrad, would bring a younger, harder face to the Kremlin: orthodox in ideology, close to the defence industry and impatient with laxity. Naming him heir skips a generation of tired old men and places the Party in the hands of a technocrat of order. What if the man from Smolny, not Gorbachev, became the Soviet Union's future?
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_heir_gorbachev: In the late 1970s, Mikhail Gorbachev has only just arrived in Moscow as Central Committee Secretary for agriculture. Naming him heir would hand power to a man not yet fifty, a generation younger than the rest of the Politburo. What if the reformer came to power years before 1985, while the economy and the empire still had reserves to spare?
COLDWAR_SOV_bre_developed_socialism_achi: The Party proclaims that the Soviet Union has entered the stage of developed socialism, a mature society that no longer needs revolutionary leaps, only steady improvement. With the borders recognised, the shelves fuller and the army mighty, the Brezhnev era appears to have reached its summit. Whether this is a plateau or the beginning of stagnation, only time will tell.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_premier_takes_the_pa: For the first time since Khrushchev, the Party and the government are united in one hand, and this time it belongs to a manager rather than an ideologue. Alexei Kosygin brings with him the ministries, the planners and the conviction that the economy, not doctrine, decides the fate of socialism. The apparatus watches warily as the Premier sets out to run the Party like a well-managed enterprise.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_baibakov_at_gosplan: Nikolai Baibakov, an oilman who has headed the State Planning Committee since 1965, knows the Soviet economy better than almost anyone. Under Kosygin, Gosplan could become the engine of reform rather than its brake, setting more realistic targets and listening to the ministries. Giving Baibakov a free hand strengthens the planners and the industrial ministries that depend on them.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_systems_men: Jermen Gvishiani, Kosygin's son-in-law and deputy head of the State Committee for Science and Technology, champions systems analysis and modern management. Through him, Soviet scientists build ties with Western research institutes and help found the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis near Vienna. Empowering these systems men brings computers, cybernetics and fresh thinking into the heart of planning.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_government_before_party: Kosygin has long been frustrated by Party secretaries who meddle in factory management without understanding production. Placing the government before the Party means letting ministries and enterprise directors make economic decisions while the apparatus confines itself to ideology and cadres. Efficiency would gain, but the regional party bosses will not easily surrender their power.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_reform_model: Everyone around Kosygin agrees that the economy needs reform; no one agrees on which. Some look to Hungary's New Economic Mechanism and market prices, others to computers and cybernetic planning that could make the plan truly scientific, still others to a careful revival of the 1965 reform within the existing system. The Premier must choose a path and stake his authority on it.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_market_socialism: Inspired by Budapest's New Economic Mechanism, Kosygin's bolder advisers propose that prices, profits and demand rather than plan targets should guide Soviet enterprises. Factories would trade among themselves, compete for customers and keep part of their earnings. Market socialism promises dynamism and better goods, while orthodox Marxists warn that it is the first step back to capitalism.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_flexible_prices: Soviet prices for bread, meat and rent have barely changed in years, held down by subsidies that cost the budget billions. Letting prices move closer to real costs would ease the endless shortages and dry up the black market, but every official remembers what happened in Novocherkassk in 1962 when meat prices rose. Flexible prices are the hardest reform of all to sell.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_enterprise_law: A new law on the socialist enterprise would give directors genuine independence: the right to draw up their own production plans, choose suppliers, hire and fire, and reinvest their profits. Ministries would become advisers rather than commanders. Productivity could rise sharply, but the trade unions fear that workers will pay for efficiency with their jobs and their bonuses.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_joint_ventures: Fiat is already building the giant car plant at Togliatti, and Western companies are eager for more Soviet contracts. Kosygin's reformers propose going further: joint ventures with Western firms on Soviet soil, financed by Western credit and run with Western know-how. Capital and technology would flow in, along with debt and a dependence on the capitalist world that hardliners find intolerable.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_cybernetic_communism: Soviet cyberneticists argue that the plan fails not because it is a plan, but because no human bureaucracy can process the millions of decisions an economy requires. Computers can. A cybernetic communism would link factories, ministries and Gosplan in a single information system that balances production in real time. The vision is breathtaking; the cost in money and machines is enormous.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_ogas_grid: Academician Viktor Glushkov of the Kiev Institute of Cybernetics has designed OGAS, the All-State Automated System for the collection and processing of information. A nationwide network of computing centres would connect thousands of enterprises with Moscow and give planners real data instead of padded reports. The bureaucracy blocked it in 1970; under Kosygin, it could finally be built.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_electronic_rouble: Viktor Glushkov's most radical idea goes beyond planning: abolish cash altogether and settle every wage and purchase electronically through the OGAS network. With every rouble traceable, the black market, embezzlement and the second economy would have nowhere to hide. Officials who live off undeclared income are, unsurprisingly, among the plan's fiercest opponents.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_planometric_institut: At the Central Economic Mathematical Institute in Moscow, economists under Nikolai Fedorenko are building optimal planning models on the foundations of Leonid Kantorovich's linear programming. Kantorovich, who will become the only Soviet Nobel laureate in economics, has shown that mathematics can allocate resources far better than guesswork. Funding these institutes would put science at the heart of Soviet planning.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_reform_within_the_plan: Kosygin's own instincts are cautious. Rather than markets or computers, he wants to rescue the reform of 1965, with its sales targets, profit indicators and enterprise incentive funds, from the ministries that have hollowed it out. Reform within the plan keeps central planning intact while giving factories just enough freedom to work better.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_profit_and_bonus: In 1962, the Kharkov economist Yevsei Liberman published an article in Pravda titled 'Plan, Profit, Bonus', arguing that enterprises should be judged by their profitability and that workers should share in it. His ideas inspired the 1965 reform before the apparatus watered them down. Reviving them would reward efficient factories and give workers a reason to care about quality.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_production_associati: In 1973, the Central Committee and the Council of Ministers order the merger of enterprises into large production associations, combining factories, design bureaus and research institutes under a single management. Done properly, these associations could cut out layers of ministerial bureaucracy and speed the path from invention to production. Done badly, they simply create bigger monopolies.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_apparatus_resists: Reform threatens the power of the regional party secretaries, the branch ministries and the thousands of officials who live by allocating scarce resources. Once again, as after 1965, the apparatus begins to sabotage the changes through delays, reinterpretations and quiet obstruction. Kosygin must now decide whether to win the Party over with concessions or to break its resistance.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_bring_the_party_along: Kosygin knows that no reform survives in the Soviet Union without the Party's blessing. By offering the nomenklatura positions in the new structures, consulting the regional secretaries and wrapping the changes in Leninist language, he can turn opponents into reluctant partners. The reform will move more slowly, but it will no longer be fought at every step.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_break_the_apparatus: Kosygin's patience is exhausted. If the apparatus will not reform, it must be removed: obstructive ministers dismissed, regional secretaries retired and the stability of cadres brought to an end. Breaking the apparatus would clear the way for real change, but it means open war with the most powerful class in the country and the risk of a backlash that could cost the Premier everything.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_curb_the_military_budget: Defence absorbs a far larger share of Soviet output than the official budget admits, starving the civilian economy of steel, engineers and investment. Kosygin argues that strategic parity has been achieved and that every additional tank is a refrigerator or a flat the people will never see. Curbing military spending would free resources, but it will turn the marshals and the defence industry against him.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_conversion_of_defence_pl: The defence plants hold the best machine tools and engineers in the Soviet Union. Converting part of their capacity to civilian production could bring quality televisions, washing machines and tractors to the market. Defence directors already make some consumer goods as a sideline; Kosygin would make it a central task, much to the displeasure of the Military-Industrial Commission.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_trade_not_tanks: Kosygin believes the future of the Soviet Union lies in commerce with the world, not confrontation. Trade agreements with France, Italy and West Germany, credits from Western banks and an end to costly adventures could do more for the image of socialism than any military parade. Trade, not tanks, would ease tensions and bring in the technology the Soviet economy badly needs.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_glassboro_spirit: In June 1967, Kosygin and President Lyndon Johnson met for three days at a small college in Glassboro, New Jersey. The summit produced no treaty, but it showed that the leaders of the two superpowers could talk frankly with each other. A new summit with the Premier could revive that spirit, ease tensions and open the way to trade, if Washington is willing to answer.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_tashkent_mediator: In January 1966, Kosygin brought India's Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistan's Ayub Khan together in Tashkent and brokered an end to their war. It was a rare triumph for Soviet diplomacy in the role of peacemaker. Renewing this role would raise Moscow's standing in South Asia and win friends in both New Delhi and Islamabad, though balancing the two rivals is never easy.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_not_a_single_soldier: In March 1979, as the communist regime in Kabul begs for Soviet troops to crush the uprising in Herat, Kosygin answers bluntly that the Soviet Union cannot replace the Afghan people in their own struggle. Holding to this line would keep the Soviet Army out of a war it cannot win, at the cost of disappointing an ally and risking its collapse.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_the_premiers_heart: Kosygin's heart is failing. A boating accident in 1976 and repeated heart attacks have weakened him, and historically he died in December 1980, only weeks after resigning. If his reforms are to outlive him, the Premier must choose who will carry them forward: a young reformer from the provinces or the disciplined chairman of the KGB.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_heir_gorbachev: Kosygin sees in the younger provincial secretaries, above all Mikhail Gorbachev of Stavropol, the men who could finish what he started. Naming Gorbachev heir would hand the reform course to a generation that believes the system can be renewed from within. What if the Premier's legacy passed directly to the future architect of perestroika?
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_heir_andropov: Kosygin and Andropov share a distaste for corruption and a belief that the economy must work better. Naming the KGB chairman heir would secure discipline and order for the reform course, though Andropov's vision is one of tighter control rather than greater freedom. What if the Premier's experiment passed into the hands of the Chekist?
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_rule_of_the_planners: If the Party cannot be reformed, perhaps it can be bypassed. In this most radical outcome, the planners and engineers of Gosplan take over the state, with Nikolai Baibakov at their head, and govern by data and expertise rather than ideology. The leading role of the Communist Party would end, replaced by a technocracy that answers to efficiency alone.
COLDWAR_SOV_kos_socialism_that_works: After years of struggle against the apparatus, the Kosygin reforms finally bear fruit: factories that meet demand, shops with goods on the shelves and growth that no longer depends on ever more labour and raw materials. For the first time since the 1950s, Soviet socialism seems able to compete with the West on its own terms.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_president_of_the_pre: For years, Nikolai Podgorny's office as head of state has been largely ceremonial: signing decrees, awarding orders and receiving foreign ambassadors. As General Secretary, he would turn the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet into a real centre of power, governing through the institutions of the state rather than through the Party apparatus. The state, not the Party, would become the face of Soviet power.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_supreme_soviet_awake: The Supreme Soviet of the USSR meets only a few days each year to approve the plan and the budget unanimously. Podgorny would give it real work: standing commissions that scrutinise ministries, deputies who question officials and debates that actually change laws. A living parliament would revive Lenin's call for all power to the soviets, though the Party secretaries will see it as a threat to their monopoly.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_kharkov_connection: Podgorny built his career in Ukraine, from the sugar industry and the Kharkov regional committee to the leadership of the Ukrainian Communist Party in Kiev. His network of Ukrainian cadres, engineers and managers remains loyal. Drawing on the Kharkov connection would strengthen the voice of the second-largest republic in Moscow and win support among those who want the union to be a true partnership of nations.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_council_of_ministers: Podgorny has no strong base in the Party Secretariat, but the branch ministries, chafing under the interference of Party secretaries, are natural allies. By promising the ministers greater autonomy and a voice in the Presidium, he can build a coalition of the state against the apparatus. The industrial ministries would gain power, and the economy a clearer chain of command.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_state_question: Podgorny must decide what kind of state he wants to build. One path leads to a genuine federation in which the union republics gain real rights and a voice in every decision that concerns them. The other leads to a strong Presidium, a central state presidency that governs the union from Moscow above both the Party and the republics. Either way, the Soviet state will never look the same.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_a_federal_union: The Soviet constitution already calls the union a voluntary federation of sovereign republics; Podgorny would make the words mean something. Republican governments would gain control over their own economies, languages and cultures, and the republics would have to approve any union decision that affects them. A federal union could win the loyalty of the non-Russian nations, or give them the tools to leave.
